parsed.explanation: The combined operative regime pairs an enforced criminal statute (Article 354, 3 months–2 years) with documented official hostility, a society where only 15% see the area as good for LGBTQ+ people, and — most weightily — police and prosecutors refusing to investigate crimes against LGBTQ+ people. An outed trans visitor thus faces credible imprisonment if conduct or presentation reads as same-sex, while assault or extortion remedies are effectively closed. No death penalty, no documented trans-specific arrests, custody violence, or document-mismatch enforcement at the border is shown, so this sits above the 0.15 tier. Non-recognition of gender means no alignment pathway, but the visitor's home documents govern entry. Adult-with-minor travel adds no documented trans-specific child exposure beyond Article 360's general provision.

entry_documents.exposure: No legal gender recognition; the dossier states a visitor's travel documents cannot be brought into line with lived gender under this country's law, so mismatch is structurally unresolved.
entry_documents.protection: Not documented. No stated border procedure, marker scrutiny, or acceptance rule for foreign documents.
entry_documents.interaction: Document/presentation mismatch feeds directly into Article 354 exposure if conduct is read as same-sex; no documented remedy at the crossing.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Article 354 criminalises conduct read as same-sex, carrying 3 months–2 years' imprisonment and fines; civil-society claim of dozens imprisoned on pretext charges is uncorroborated. Enforcement willingness predates 2017 (2013 arrests, prison sentences).
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Appeal existed in the 2013 case (suspended sentences after outcry), but no trans-specific custody protection documented.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Detention would occur under a regime where police already decline LGBTQ+ cases, so custody protections are weak.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: No documented facility, ward, or custody-placement rule specific to trans visitors.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Not documented; any hospitalisation would occur within a healthcare setting where hostility toward LGBTQ+ people is documented, raising outing risk.

care_services.exposure: Documented discrimination and hostility in healthcare access (blood-donation example), reflecting staff-level anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes reaching any visitor seeking care.
care_services.protection: Not documented. No equality or anti-discrimination law covers gender identity.
care_services.interaction: Emergency care or medication need would force disclosure into a hostile service environment with no legal recourse.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Official hostility on record: a former prime minister defended criminalisation on religious grounds; religious, women's and youth groups petitioned for harsher punishment in 2013; LGBTQ+ people framed as threats to family and procreation, homosexuality seen as foreign invention.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: State framing licenses police and public hostility toward an outed visitor and undercuts any complaint.

minors_guardians.exposure: Article 360 penalises same-sex sexual touching/relationships with under-18s (1–3 years); family coercion of LGBTQ+ identity documented but resident-facing.
minors_guardians.interaction: A trans parent travelling with a minor risks heightened scrutiny if their presentation or relationship reads as same-sex; no documented child-specific trans procedure.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Police and prosecutors refuse to investigate or prosecute crimes against LGBTQ+ people — an outed visitor who is assaulted, extorted or blackmailed has effectively no state recourse. Documented prosecution willingness (2013) and hostile social attitudes (15% acceptance) raise street risk.
street_violence_police_response.protection: No trans-specific violence statistics exist; Article 350(i) aggravates rape by orientation but its application is unstated.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Hostile society plus closed police remedy means private violence goes unredressed for a visible foreign visitor.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No anti-discrimination law; police refusal documented; no legal gender recognition. Uncorroborated imprisonment figure and unsampled 2024 survey add uncertainty rather than evidence.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Appeal in the 2013 case followed community outcry — intermittent, not institutional.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Recourse depends on public sympathy toward the accused, which the attitudinal record suggests is absent for LGBTQ+ people.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar structure: an operative criminal provision reachable by gender-nonconforming visitors, brief custodial exposure, slow remedies, and no credible execution. Higher than 0.15 anchors because no custody violence or capital clause is documented; comparable to 0.25-C's cross-dressing arrest exposure, though here the additional refusal to investigate crimes against LGBTQ+ pushes it to the lower end of that tier.

Lower than 0.35-B: that anchor describes stops, hours-long interviews and fines with detention rarely becoming imprisonment. Here a standing penal statute with imprisonment and fines is the documented operative rule, plus closed police remedy for victims — a more severe and more certain consequence than discretionary street checks.

Higher than 0.15-B: that anchor combines entry denial, crowded cells, withheld medical care, delayed habeas and credible capital reach. This dossier documents no custody brutality, no border exclusion rule and no death penalty — imprisonment is credible but not routine, and the 2013 sentences were suspended on appeal.

Materially lower than 0.55-B: that anchor's harm is administrative — secondary screening, refused admission, return transport with written reasons and appeal. Here discovery can trigger criminal prosecution under Article 354 and victims cannot reach police, a categorically higher severity than discretionary administrative refusal.

parsed.synthesis: The regime's operative core is criminalisation plus closed recourse: Article 354 makes any same-sex-read conduct punishable by imprisonment, while the documented refusal of police and prosecutors to investigate crimes against LGBTQ+ people removes the ordinary protective layer a traveller relies on after discovery. Official hostility (a former prime minister's religious defence, organised petitions for harsh punishment) and a society where only 15% of residents see their area as good for LGBTQ+ people combine law and social climate in the same direction, so passing or silence is the traveller's only buffer — and it evaporates at any document, care or police encounter. Mitigating factors are real but limited: no death penalty, no documented trans-specific arrests, custody brutality or border screening practice, and an appeal that once produced suspended sentences. Those keep the rating out of the 0.15 band; the enforced statute, state hostility and absent remedy hold it firmly in High Risk. For an adult travelling with a minor, Article 360 and added scrutiny raise exposure at the margin, but no child-specific trans rule is documented.
